summary: A 1975 commentary on using procedure calls as a network protocol. It discusses issues in building distributed computing systems and the shortcomings of RFC 674. See also RFC 542 and RFC 354.

plainLanguage.summary: This note thinks about letting one computer call a task on another like a function, and lists what might go wrong.

questions: remote procedure call versus message passing
subtitle: An early argument that distributed systems should be built on message passing, not remote procedure calls.

tldr.problem: The Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) of RFC 674 treats a network of machines as one program calling procedures, with a single point of control.
tldr.mechanism: The commentary argues that autonomous cooperating processes exchanging requests and replies over communication paths are a better model, and lists ten specific weaknesses of PCP.
tldr.outcome: The authors accept PCP may serve the National Software Works project but object to it becoming the de-facto network standard for distributed computation.

today: RFC 684 is an opinion piece from April 1975 and its unit metadata lists the status as Unknown, with no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records one side of an early debate about RFC 674.

sections.title: Why the Commentary Was Written
sections.content:
RFC 684 is a critique of the Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) set out in RFC 674. It is meant to start a dialog on how to design a distributed computing system. The author says earlier suggestions to the PCP designers dealt with implementation details, some of which became part of PCP Version 2; this note targets the concepts underneath.

The authors do not object to PCP being the base for the National Software Works (NSW) project, since it is too late for that. They object to the "PCP philosophy" becoming the standard for distributed computation.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone wrote a polite but firm note saying a popular plan has a flawed idea at its heart, hoping to change how future plans are made.

sections.title: Procedure Calls versus Message Passing
sections.content:
The core objection is PCP's premise that procedure calling is the starting point for multi-computer systems. That yields a model with one central point of algorithm control, rather than independent entities cooperating over shared communication paths. The authors prefer a request and reply protocol, where actions are asked for indirectly, preserving the integrity of each process.

They note that a local procedure call is cheap, often one machine instruction, while a remote call needs a great deal of work, and blurring the two is unwise. Interprocess communication differs much less between local and remote cases. They also argue that network techniques should be applied to local computation, not the other way around.
sections.plainLanguage: Calling a function next door is quick, but calling one across the country is a big job. Pretending they are the same hides that. Asking politely by message makes the distance obvious.

sections.title: Ten Particular Weaknesses
sections.content:
The RFC lists ten situations where PCP looks weak. Among them:

  • Recovering from component failure is hard for a process that is only being manipulated by a controller.
  • One process can change another's environment, or cause arbitrary procedures to run, without that process taking part, which hurts modularity and error containment.
  • It models long-running parallel activity and requests with multiple returns poorly.
  • Communication paths are not abstract objects and cannot be passed to an inferior without creating a new connection.
  • It seems too complicated for short, periodic exchanges or for small hosts, and no minimum implementation is defined.
  • A malicious user could splice to a service and make it overflow its table space.
  • It is unclear whether PCP is an implementation virtual machine or an application virtual machine; the authors feel neither goal is fully met.
sections.plainLanguage: The list says the boss-and-helper style makes errors hard to handle, lets one machine meddle with another, is clumsy for long jobs, and is too heavy for small computers.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: The authors conclude that procedure calling is not the appropriate basis for distributed multi-computer systems because it can neither directly nor accurately model the network environment. They add that the PCP virtual programming system may be inadequate for many distributed systems because the complexities and possibilities unique to networks are not provided for at this basic level.
sections.plainLanguage: In short: use messages between independent helpers, because that matches how networks really behave.
